explanation:
## Employee salary vs freelance billing: what the numbers actually compare

Going freelance is rarely a simple raise. A higher hourly rate has to cover everything an employer used to absorb: paid leave, employer-side taxes, health insurance, retirement matching, and the gaps between contracts. This calculator puts both paths on the same yearly footing so you compare take-home against take-home, not gross salary against an optimistic day rate.

## How the calculation works

- **Employee side**: monthly gross salary annualized into net employee income.
- **Freelance side**: hourly rate x billable hours per month x 12, converted from USD at the MEP exchange rate you enter.
- **Difference**: freelance annual minus employee annual, so a positive number means freelancing pays more on these inputs.

The single lever most people get wrong is **billable hours**. You cannot bill 160 hours a month — sales, admin, invoicing, and downtime eat 25-40% of your working week.

## Billable-hours reality check

| Hours worked / month | Realistic billable | Utilization | What eats the rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| 160 (full-time) | 110-130 | 70-80% | Admin, sales, invoicing |
| 160 (early-stage) | 60-90 | 40-55% | Prospecting, unpaid pitches |
| 80 (part-time) | 55-65 | 70-80% | Context-switching overhead |

*Set billable hours, not calendar hours, in the field above — that is the most common reason people overestimate freelance income.*

## What the freelance rate has to absorb

- **No paid time off**: ~20 vacation days + holidays + sick days is roughly 5-6 unbilled weeks a year. Price it in.
- **Self-employment tax burden**: freelancers usually owe both halves of social contributions plus income tax. Set aside 25-35% of gross before treating money as yours.
- **Insurance and retirement**: an employer match and group health plan can be worth 15-25% of salary that you now fund alone.
- **Income gaps**: client churn means months at lower utilization. Keep a 3-6 month buffer so a slow quarter is not a crisis.

## When freelancing actually wins

Freelancing tends to beat employment once your effective rate clears roughly 1.5x your equivalent hourly employee wage and you can sustain utilization above ~65%. Below that, the higher rate is just compensating for lost benefits and downtime, and your real take-home can land under the salaried equivalent.

## Important disclaimer

This is a reference estimate based on the numbers you enter. Tax treatment of self-employment versus employment varies by country and personal situation; confirm with an accountant before making a career switch. Values reviewed for 2026.

faq.q: Do freelancers earn more than employees?
faq.a: It depends on your hourly rate, billable hours per month, and tax situation. Use this calculator to compare directly with your specific numbers.

faq.q: What counts as billable hours for freelancers?
faq.a: Hours spent directly on client work. Typical range is 80-120 hours per month. The rest goes to business development, administration, and planning.

faq.q: What are the main differences in employee benefits?
faq.a: Employees receive a steady salary, paid time off, health insurance, and employer-matched retirement contributions. Freelancers must cover these separately.

faq.q: How should I set my freelance hourly rate?
faq.a: Calculate your target annual income, add your tax burden and business costs, then divide by billable hours. Factor in vacation, sick days, and downtime.

faq.q: How much do taxes differ for freelancers vs employees?
faq.a: Freelancers typically pay self-employment tax plus income tax. Employees have payroll taxes deducted automatically. Freelancers often owe more overall.

faq.q: Do freelancers get paid time off?
faq.a: No. Days off mean no income. Budget carefully for vacations, holidays, and sick days when setting your rate and planning billable hours.

faq.q: What about health insurance and retirement for freelancers?
faq.a: Freelancers must obtain their own health insurance and retirement plans. These are essential ongoing costs, separate from your income.
Freelance income is less stable than employment. It varies based on project availability and client relationships. Build an emergency fund.

referenceTables.title: Freelance Hourly Rate Needed to Match a Salary (US, 2026)
referenceTables.note: Fuente: derived from the standard W-2→1099 conversion rule (IRS self-employment tax 15.3% on the first $184,500 for 2026, SSA wage base) plus typical benefit loads. Base rate = salary ÷ 2,080 work-hours/yr. The 1.25× multiplier just offsets the employer half of FICA you now pay yourself; the 1.5× multiplier also covers ~5–6 weeks of unpaid time off, individual health insurance ($450–$700/mo), and the lost 401(k) match. These rates assume billable hours, not calendar hours — see the utilization table above.
referenceTables.caption: Don't compare a freelance rate to a salary directly: a $100k salaried job needs a $60–72/h freelance rate just to break even after self-employment tax and lost benefits.
